detaileddescription.para: A high-performance, multi-tenant healthcare backend written in modern C++20. Valhalla exposes a versioned REST API for managing medical service providers (clinics, laboratories, pharmacies, radiology centers), their staff, patients, visits, and appointments — with authentication, role-based permissions, and built-in abuse protection baked into the request pipeline.

blockquote.para: Status: Active development. The API surface and data model are still evolving.
Documentation & code architecture: The generated Doxygen reference documents the C++ API, class hierarchy, and source layout. For the HTTP API itself, see Interactive API docs.

sect1.title: Quick Start
sect1.para: Run the server with its own bundled PostgreSQL in a container, using Docker or Apple Container (Apple Silicon Macs). You need one of them installed, plus curl (and python3 with Apple Container). The tool checks and tells you what's missing.
1. Install the vdt command — the Valhalla Deployment Tool (no checkout needed):

This downloads the latest tool from this repository: the vdt command goes in ~/.local/bin and its files in ~/.local/share/vdt. It adds ~/.local/bin to PATH (if it isn't already) and tab completion in ~/.zshrc and/or ~/.bashrc. Open a new terminal afterwards.

Settings: the installer creates ~/.local/share/vdt/config (.env format) with defaults for a small local container (2 server threads, 2 database connections, and raised rate limits so the API docs' Benchmark and Test console panels don't get you blocked). Every variable in it is passed to the server (see Configuration); edit it and run vdt update to apply. A .env in the directory you run vdt from is used instead (e.g. in your checkout of this repository).

Update the tool with vdt install (or vdt install v1.2.3 for a specific tag): it downloads the new version first, and only then removes the current copy and installs, so a failed download changes nothing. vdt version shows what's installed. Remove it with vdt uninstall, which works offline. Both keep your .env and dumps/.

From a checkout of this repository, ./scripts/vdt/valhalla.sh is the same tool (the installed vdt command is this file under another name). Details: Manage it with valhalla.sh. Without the tool: Run with Docker. To build and run natively: Getting Started.

REST API (v2) built on the Drogon asynchronous web framework.
Multi-tenant service model — a single deployment serves multiple service types (clinics, laboratories, pharmacies, radiology centers) through generic, type-parameterized controllers.
People & clients — separate User and Provider client types, each with full create / login / logout / read / update / delete / search lifecycles.
Patients, visits & appointments — patient records, health data, prescriptions, drugs, paid services, and visit/appointment scheduling per service.
Staff management — invite, add, and remove staff members on a per-service basis.
JWT authentication — stateless session tokens issued and validated via jwt-cpp.
Role-based access control — bitmask permission levels (CAN_READ, CAN_WRITE, CAN_DELETE, IS_ADMIN, IS_OWNER, IS_SUPER) enforced by a permission manager.

Security gatekeeper layered into the request flow:
DoS / rate-limiting detector with configurable rate limits, ban durations, and IP whitelist/blacklist.
Every SQL value is a bound parameter (pqxx::params); identifiers come from schema-validated keys or allowlists.
Password hashing with libsodium (Argon2id), off the request threads.
Session and token managers.

PostgreSQL persistence via Drogon's asynchronous orm::DbClient by default (DB_ASYNC=true; writes wrapped in transactions), with the legacy libpqxx connection pool, watchdog and schema validator kept behind DB_ASYNC=false for one release.
CORS support with pre-routing OPTIONS handling and standard CORS headers on every response.
Structured logging through spdlog, to console and/or file.
12-factor configuration — every setting is read from environment variables with sensible defaults.

sect1.title: Architecture
sect1.para: Requests flow through a layered pipeline. Drogon's IO threads only parse, route and answer.

By default (DB_ASYNC=true) database work runs as coroutines on the IO threads over Drogon's asynchronous orm::DbClient — no DB worker pool, and a slow query never holds a request thread. Password hashing and login checks still run on the dedicated password worker pool. The legacy synchronous path (DB executor + connection pool, DB_ASYNC=false) is kept for one release as a fallback.

listitem.para: Routes (src/api/v2/routes) declare endpoints and mark each as SECURE or INSECURE. A small registry maps a path parameter (e.g. clientType, serviceType) to the concrete controller, so one route class serves many entity types. executeControllerMethod submits the whole controller call to the DB executor, with the request data, arguments and response callback captured by value, because the answer is sent from a worker thread.
Controllers (src/controllers) implement CRUD/search logic against a generic base.
Entities (src/entities) model the domain: people (users, providers), services (clinics, laboratories, pharmacies, radiology centers), patients, visits, and appointments.

Gatekeeper (src/gatekeeper) holds the cross-cutting security concerns: DoS detector, token and session managers, the permission manager with its idle-expiry cache, and password hashing (Argon2id, with legacy scrypt hashes still accepted at login).

Concurrency (src/concurrency) has BoundedExecutor, the fixed-size thread pool with a bounded queue that submit() never blocks on. The DB executor (src/database/dbexecutor, legacy DB_ASYNC=false path) and the password worker are two instances. With zero workers a task runs inline, which the unit tests use.

Database (src/database) has the asynchronous client wrapper (AsyncDbClient, the default DB_ASYNC=true path), the legacy connection pool (BlockingPool, waits with a timeout and throws DatabaseBusy, which becomes 503), the watchdog that reconnects dropped connections, and the handler that borrows a connection for one query.
Configurator (src/configurator) loads and validates configuration from the environment at startup.

Store (src/store) provides shared singleton object access. Objects built for every request use Store::cachedObject<T>(), which keeps a per-thread pointer and only goes back to the Store when an object has been replaced (tests replace the database controller with a fake).

sect2.title: Run with Docker
sect2.para: Every release tag publishes an all-in-one image to Docker Hub: the server plus its own PostgreSQL, so no external database is needed. It is a single multi-arch image (linux/amd64 and linux/arm64); Docker and Apple Container pull the right one automatically. It's meant for demos, testing, and CI.

blockquote.para: Which should I use? The Docker image works on any OS. The Alpine tarballs attached to each GitHub Release run only on Alpine Linux. Anywhere else, without Docker, build from source.

The database is ephemeral. Every container start, including a restart, begins with a fresh, empty database initialised from init.sql. Nothing is kept. For persistent data, run the server against your own PostgreSQL instead (see Run the server).

sect2.para: Build the image yourself from the repository root:

The build compiles every C++ dependency from source on Alpine and runs the unit tests; the build fails if a test fails. The first build takes a long time; later builds reuse the cached dependency layer until conanfile.txt or conan.lock changes.

Release downloads. Each GitHub Release also attaches server-alpine-amd64.tar.gz and server-alpine-arm64.tar.gz. These are built on Alpine (musl libc) and only run on Alpine-based systems; everywhere else use the Docker image, or build from source.

scripts/vdt/valhalla.sh wraps the commands above for both Docker and Apple Container. It picks Apple Container when it's installed and Docker otherwise (force one with --runtime docker or --runtime container).

Install it as the vdt command (no checkout needed). This downloads the latest valhalla.sh, the API test scripts and their payloads from this repository. The command goes in ~/.local/bin/vdt (a link); the files go in ~/.local/share/vdt, without the .sh extension (vdt, test_api, schemathesis_test) and executable, plus a copy of the installer. It adds ~/.local/bin to PATH (if it isn't already) and tab completion in ~/.zshrc and/or ~/.bashrc:

Then open a new terminal and use vdt instead of ./scripts/vdt/valhalla.sh (e.g. vdt run, vdt status). Afterwards the tool manages itself with the same installer. The installer keeps a copy of itself next to the tool, so uninstall works offline; install downloads the latest installer first, then uninstalls the current copy and installs the new one (if the download fails, nothing is removed):
The installed copy has everything except build, which needs a full checkout of the repository. From a checkout, every command works the same as ./scripts/vdt/valhalla.sh <command>:

Options go before or after the command: --name, --port, --runtime, --env-file, -n/--dry-run (see what any command would change, without changing anything), -y/--yes and -p/--persist / --no-persist (see Persistence below). The first time you run it, it adds tab completion to ~/.zshrc and/or ~/.bashrc; open a new terminal to use it (set VALHALLA_NO_COMPLETION=1 to skip).
Each command first checks the tools it needs (curl, python3 for Apple Container, jq for test, fzf for payload, …) and lists any that are missing, with how to install them.
Every run, update and restart waits until /api/v2/hello answers and prints the version line from the log.

It passes every variable in a settings file to the container, using the first it finds: .env in the directory you run it from, .env next to the script (your checkout), or ~/.local/share/vdt/config (same format). The installer creates that last one with defaults for a small local container: SERVER_THREADS = 2, DB_MAX_CONN = 2, and raised MAX_REQUESTS/MAX_FPS. It's yours from then on: kept on update, and on uninstall unless it's still the unedited default. The script itself hard-codes no server settings; anything no .env sets falls back to the server's defaults (4 threads, 10 connections, MAX_REQUESTS 10000, MAX_FPS 100). Only one file is used; they aren't merged. Variables set in the shell win over .env for a single run (SERVER_THREADS=4 ./scripts/vdt/valhalla.sh update). Quoted values, spaces around = and # comments are fine. After editing .env, run ./scripts/vdt/valhalla.sh update to apply it. Use another file with --env-file path (or VALHALLA_ENV_FILE), or skip it with --env-file none.

Disk space. After update and build, the tool removes its own older images that no container uses: never the image the new container runs, and never the -deps build image. It then frees leftover layers. On Docker that's only the dangling images that came from this repository; Apple Container can't tell where an image came from, so there it runs container image prune, which removes only dangling (untagged, unused) images. It reports the image disk usage before and after. -n shows what it would remove, and --no-prune (or VALHALLA_NO_PRUNE=1) keeps everything.

Update notices. Every few hours (VALHALLA_UPDATE_INTERVAL, default 6 hours) a background job checks, when you're online, whether Docker Hub has a newer image than your container runs and whether GitHub has a newer version of the tool than your installed copy. The next commands then show a small table with the installed and latest versions and the command that updates them: vdt update covers both — the image and the vdt tool itself (it runs the installer after the container is recreated). vdt install only updates the tool, and vdt update --image-only / --tool-only pick one side. The check never delays a command. The exception is vdt status, which checks right away when there's an internet connection (a second or two) and ends with an Updates: line: up to date, available (with the table), or not checked when offline. The table only appears in an interactive terminal, styled as far as it supports: colors, Unicode box drawing, emoji, or Nerd Font icons at level 2 (VALHALLA_NERD=1 forces them). Turn it off with VALHALLA_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1. A checkout, or a copy installed from one, isn't checked for tool updates.

Login token secret. TOKEN_SECRET signs the JWT login tokens, and the tool never lets it change by itself between starts (which would log everyone out). The installer generates one into ~/.local/share/vdt/config. A container gets the first of: --token-secret, TOKEN_SECRET in the shell, the .env in use, ~/.local/share/vdt/config (checked even when a .env is in use), or the replaced container's secret. If there's none, one is generated once and saved to config. vdt env shows which one is used, and vdt secret replaces it (asking first).

Persistence. Without it, the bundled database starts from init.sql on every container start. Add --persist once (vdt run --persist, vdt update --persist, or VALHALLA_PERSIST=1 in .env) and the database is kept in ~/.local/share/vdt/dumps/<name>-persist.sql, which is mounted into the container. The image's entrypoint loads it at start instead of init.sql and saves it whenever the container stops, including restarts outside the tool (Docker Desktop, a reboot). The tool also saves it before stop, restart, update, build and delete (the previous dump is kept as .prev), and if that save fails, nothing is stopped. The setting is stored in the container, so later commands remember it; --no-persist turns it off. vdt status shows whether it's on and when the database was last saved. Restoring a dump made by a different image prints a warning, because if that image changed the schema the old schema comes back. Images released before this feature still work: the tool restores the dump itself after the container starts.

In a terminal, vdt messages and help (or --help) use colors, Unicode box drawing, BMP symbols and emoji as far as the terminal supports them, and help is paged with less when it's longer than the screen; piped or with NO_COLOR=1 output is plain text. Force a style with VALHALLA_FANCY=0 (plain) to 3 (everything).
Full help (./scripts/vdt/valhalla.sh help):

sect1.title: API Overview
sect1.para: All endpoints live under the /api/v2 prefix (for example http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/v2/hello). Routes marked 🔒 require a valid Authorization: Bearer <token> header (obtained from /clients/{type}/login); 🔓 routes are public. Request and response bodies are JSON.

sect2.title: Interactive API docs
sect2.para: The server ships its own API documentation, compiled into the binary:

entry.para: Swagger UI for every endpoint, plus an API Guide panel (permissions, data model, validation, errors, rate limiting, recipes, troubleshooting) and a Test console that runs all endpoints in order against the live server with dummy data, and a Benchmark panel (latency percentiles and requests/s per endpoint; writes are created with unique data and deleted afterwards)

sect2.para: With the defaults that is http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/v2/doc; the startup banner prints the exact URL. From the page you can also download the OpenAPI 3 spec and a Postman collection (also kept in docs/openapi.json and docs/valhalla.postman_collection.json).

The page is embedded into the binary, and every cmake --build regenerates it from tools/docs/ first (the valhalla_docs target) (this needs bash, python3 and Node.js/npm; if one is missing, the committed docs/api.html is embedded as is). Pass -DVALHALLA_BUILD_DOCS=OFF to skip regeneration. To regenerate by hand:
To include real response samples in the docs, run SAMPLES_OUT=tests/api_tests/samples.jsonl ./scripts/test/test_api.sh against a running server before tools/docs/build.sh.

sect2.title: Staff — /staff/services/{serviceType}/staff/...
sect2.para: These routes are registered with Drogon's METHOD_ADD (src/api/v2/routes/staff.hpp), which puts the controller path (/api/v2/staff) in front, hence the doubled staff segment. The interactive docs still show the shorter /services/{serviceType}/staff/... form, which does not match the server.

sect2.title: Clinic records — /clinic/{resource}/...
sect2.para: Each resource supports create (POST), read (POST), update (PUT) and delete (DELETE) under /clinic/{resource}/, all 🔒. Resources:
delete is not supported for health, patientdrugs, reports, requests, prescriptions and paidservices; they are removed with their parent record.

sect2.title: Appointments — /appointments/{serviceType}/... (serviceType ∈ clinics, pharmacies, laboratories, radiologycenters)
sect2.para: The interactive docs currently only show the clinics variant.

blockquote.para: Unknown routes return a JSON 404 ("Endpoint not found."). Rate-limit, ban and blacklist replies from the DoS filter are plain text.

sect1.title: Front-end development (CORS and Docker)
sect1.para: The API listens on http://localhost:8080. CORS is open: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *, no credentials, methods GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, HEAD, OPTIONS, request headers Content-Type, Authorization, Accept, X-Requested-With (a preflight echoes Access-Control-Request-Headers), and exposed response headers Retry-After, Content-Length. Preflight responses are cached for 7200 seconds.

In Docker bridge mode every request arrives from one gateway IP, so the rate limiter treats all front-end traffic as a single client. On native Linux Docker that address is often 172.17.0.1, but on Docker Desktop for macOS or Windows it is usually different. There is no existing log line that prints the peer IP. Without code changes, use one of these instead: on native Linux, docker network inspect bridge and its Gateway; run docker exec <container> sh -c 'ss -tn' or read /proc/net/tcp inside the container while a host curl is in flight to see the peer address; or use docker logs <container> after a request. On Docker Desktop for macOS or Windows the address is usually not the bridge gateway.

Whitelist entries are unanchored regular expressions, so 172.17.0.1 also matches 172.17.0.10 through 172.17.0.199. To whitelist only the gateway, anchor the pattern. In a shell or --env-file value the backslashes stay literal:
In a dotenv or compose file the same value is written without extra escaping:
Raise the dev rate limits as well (MAX_REQUESTS, MAX_FPS) if React StrictMode double requests trip the limiter. A commented example for a dev .env (no secrets):

Put these settings where the container or server actually reads them: a project .env for the native binary, --env-file FILE / VALHALLA_ENV_FILE for valhalla.sh, or -e / --env-file for docker run. docker/entrypoint.sh reads them from the process environment.
WHITELIST disables DoS checks for matching IPs, so it is for development only. Never whitelist a broad pattern in production.

sect2.title: Browser simulation
sect2.para: ./scripts/test/cors_react_check.sh simulates what a browser does before and after cross-origin calls from a React dev server. It runs on macOS's default bash 3.2 (arrays and read -a are supported there) and uses only POSIX-ish sed, awk, tr and grep calls.

Headless Chromium against the page reported all 7 calls as PASS (HTTP 400/401/200, nothing blocked by the browser). The --credentials variant is expected to fail with the wildcard-origin message; that is the documented limitation, not a regression.

To run ./scripts/test/cors_test.sh --strict against cases that need low DoS thresholds, start separate server instances on different ports (a banned IP stays banned, so 429 and 503 cannot both be provoked on the same instance):

run_release.sh loads ENV_FILE and exports every value from it, so settings in the file override the shell environment. Set ENV_FILE=none to use the command-line variables, or create one file per instance with a heredoc in a temporary directory (tmpdir=$(mktemp -d)).
Then run the matching case against each instance:
Each instance proves its targeted case. The other cases are skipped there by design.

sect2.title: Known limitation: malformed requests (HTTP 400)
sect2.para: Drogon 1.9.14 writes the response for a malformed request line (for example GET /bad http/1.1) directly to the connection during parsing. That path bypasses both the custom error handler and the pre-sending advice, so these 400 responses contain no CORS headers. No supported hook adds headers there in this Drogon version, so front-end code that triggers such an error will still see a browser CORS failure.

listitem.para: Code style: enforced via .clang-format; static analysis configured through .clang-tidy and cppcheck.supp.
Editor support: .clangd provides LSP configuration; .vscode/ and .zed/ settings are included. CMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS is on, so compile_commands.json is generated for tooling.
Warnings: built with -Wall -Wextra -pedantic.
Versioning: the current Git tag is embedded into the binary at build time via get_tag.sh.

Dependencies: conan.lock pins the exact version and recipe revision of every Conan package, for the Alpine Docker builds (amd64 and arm64) and for local macOS/Linux builds. Conan uses it automatically. To change or update dependencies, edit conanfile.txt if needed, run tools/conan/update_lock.sh, and commit both files. Don't use a plain conan lock create .: it locks only your own platform, and the Docker build would then fail.

Build options: -DENABLE_TESTS=OFF skips the unit tests (default ON); -DVALHALLA_BUILD_DOCS=OFF skips regenerating the API docs (default ON); -DVALHALLA_BUILD_DOXYGEN=OFF skips generating the Doxygen reference (default ON, ignored if Doxygen is not installed). Debug builds on Linux enable AddressSanitizer, UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer and LeakSanitizer.

Tests: a Catch2 suite lives in tests/. It runs without a database, so it works on any machine. build.sh runs it through the conan-debug/conan-release CTest presets, and building the Docker image runs it too, on Alpine.

sect2.title: Source documentation
sect2.para: The C++ source is documented with Doxygen: every class, function and non-obvious implementation detail has a Doxygen-compatible comment. See docs/ARCHITECTURE.md for the component map and docs/CONTRIBUTING.md for the documentation conventions. The HTML/XML reference is generated by the valhalla_doxygen CMake target, which runs on every cmake --build when Doxygen is available. The result is published under docs/doxygen/ (HTML and XML, tracked alongside the API docs). Doxygen excludes that directory from its own input, so it never documents its output:
docs/index.html redirects to that page, so serving the docs/ directory as static files gives a single entry point for the published documentation.
Pass -DVALHALLA_BUILD_DOXYGEN=OFF to skip the target. To generate by hand, create the output directory first (Doxygen writes its warning log there):

sect1.title: Contributing
sect1.para: Contributions are welcome. Please open an issue to discuss substantial changes first, keep commits focused, and run clang-format before submitting a pull request.
